content.p: Martin Eric Stephens was a 29-year-old catering worker from the Illawarra coast of New South Wales when Indonesian police arrested him in the departure lounge of Bali's international airport in April 2005. Heroin was strapped to his body. He was one of nine young Australians seized in a single operation that the press named the Bali Nine, and in February 2006 a Denpasar court sentenced him to life imprisonment for his part in the plot.

He spent almost two decades in Indonesian prisons. His lawyers argued that he was a minor figure, and an Australian police letter backed that view, but the courts did not change his sentence. Unlike the group's two organisers, who were executed in 2015, he lived to be sent home. On 15 December 2024 he and four other prisoners were flown out of Bali to Darwin.
content.h2: A catering job and a trip to Bali
content.p: Stephens came from Towradgi, near Wollongong. The Senior, a regional news outlet, described him as a former junior lifesaver and local footballer. His mother, Michele, was told by an Australian consular official on 19 April 2005 that her son was in a Bali jail on suspicion of drug smuggling, according to the paper's timeline.

By then he was working for a Sydney catering company alongside several of the people who would end up in the same case. The Age reported that Renae Lawrence, who worked in logistics at the firm, counted him as one of her friends there. Matthew Norman and Andrew Chan also worked for the same catering business, according to the paper's profiles of the accused. His parents described him in public as a loving, hard-working son, and friends and neighbours told reporters they could not believe he would be involved in heroin smuggling.

Police alleged that Chan was the recruiter. The Age reported that police said he had promised members of the group 10,000 US dollars each on delivery of the heroin in Sydney, paid their air fares and hotel bills and given them spending money. Stephens and Lawrence booked into room 126 at the Kuta Laguna hotel. By the day of the arrests they were staying in room 124 of another hotel, the Dharma, according to the same newspaper.

Indonesian police made the arrests on Sunday 17 April 2005, after a tip from the Australian Federal Police. Four people were taken in the boarding lounge at Ngurah Rai airport with heroin strapped around their waists: Stephens, Lawrence, and two young men from Brisbane, Scott Rush and Michael Czugaj. The Age called them the "airport four". Four others, Myuran Sukumaran, Tach Duc Thanh Nguyen, Si Yi Chen and Norman, were arrested at the Melasti Hotel, where police found scales, packaging and 350 grams of heroin. Chan was arrested alone as he boarded a flight to Sydney.

The total seized from the four at the airport was 8.3 kilograms, according to The Age. Sources differ on how much was on Stephens himself. ABC News and SBS said 2.9 kilograms was strapped to his legs and stomach, while the Sydney Morning Herald in 2006 put the figure at 3.3 kilograms. The Age's first reports said the airport four faced the possibility of execution if convicted, and the four in the hotel faced ten years.

The Age also noted that the Bali police, at that stage, could not say who had supplied the drugs, and that they had struggled to deny the suggestion that undercover agents had sold the heroin to the Australians. The paper said the "mules" who carry drugs across borders are normally the least important targets of any investigation.

Stephens gave statements to police. According to The Age's later reconstruction, he and Lawrence both heard Chan say he knew the federal police had him in their sights, and Stephens said he overheard a phone call from which he concluded that Chan was being followed and did not dare leave on 14 April. The same reconstruction reported that Chan changed his number and told the others to change hotels on 13 April.

The cases of the nine did not all finish on one day. Judgments were handed down in February 2006. The Sydney Morning Herald reported that Chan received a death sentence, that Sukumaran later received the same penalty, and that Stephens and Czugaj were each sentenced to life imprisonment. The presiding judge in Chan's case, Arief Supratman, referred to a letter from the Australian Federal Police nominating Chan as the ringleader. The court dismissed claims that four other defendants had been forced to act as couriers by Chan's threats to kill their families, according to the newspaper. A police video from 2005, quoted by The Age, had shown Lawrence urging others not to name the people she called "Mr Bigs" for fear of reprisals against their families.

The verdicts caused a diplomatic row. Prime Minister John Howard said it was beyond him that anyone could be "so stupid", and begged young Australians not to take such a risk. Australian Federal Police Commissioner Mick Keelty refused to apologise for tipping off Indonesia, saying the force would "do the same thing again". Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said ministers had made private pleas in December and January to Indonesia to ask prosecutors not to seek the death penalty.

Stephens's own sentence was a life term, and the ABC's later profile said it carried no hope of release. It was not cut on appeal. The Senior's timeline records that the High Court in Bali rejected his appeal and confirmed the sentence on 27 April 2006. The Sydney Morning Herald reported in December that year that the Supreme Court had also upheld it.

Stephens served the early part of his sentence in Kerobokan prison on Bali. In December 2006 the Sydney Morning Herald met Christine Winarni Puspayanti, a 31-year-old from Java who had converted from Islam to Christianity in 2004. She said she had met Stephens in June 2005, when she and other members of her church began visiting inmates, and that he gave her a silver friendship ring. She brought him breakfast every day, and said their plan was to marry in the prison in March or April 2007. Her Muslim parents had at first objected, she said. The prison governor, Ilham Djaya, said there was no prohibition on a wedding, but that there could be no honeymoon. Stephens's mother said the family loved Puspayanti but that their focus was a judicial review of the sentence. The Senior later recorded that they married in a traditional prison ceremony in 2011, in front of his parents and guests.

By 2010 the legal effort turned to the argument that he had been a minor player. SBS reported in April 2010 that his lawyers had lodged a request for judicial review at the Denpasar District Court, citing as new evidence a letter from the Australian Federal Police describing him as a minor figure in the plot. In January 2011 the ABC reported that three Supreme Court judges had rejected his final appeal. Stephens had argued that he did not organise the ring. Mick Keelty, by then a former commissioner, had given a written statement calling him a minor player, but a court spokesman said it could not be used as evidence. The ABC added that his last chance of clemency would be an appeal to Indonesia's president. By that time Stephens was 34.

Around him the group was thinning. Chan and Sukumaran were executed in April 2015. Lawrence, who had a 20-year sentence, was released in 2018, the same year Nguyen died of cancer in custody. In 2020 the Indonesia Expat quoted Stephens, as the ABC later recounted, saying that he hoped for release so that he could look after his wife and daughter.

Talk of letting the surviving prisoners serve their time in Australia had circulated for years. When it surfaced again in November 2024, Stephens's parents, Michele and Bill, kept their own counsel, The Senior said, and recalled that Michele had said in 2007 that she had "seen and heard it all before". By then, the paper said, he was 48 and had been jailed for more than 7,000 days. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese raised the case with Indonesia's new president, Prabowo Subianto, at the APEC summit in Peru, as Reuters reported. Trade Minister Don Farrell said at the time that the proposal was not to release the men, but to have them serve their sentences in Australia.

On Sunday 15 December 2024 Stephens, Rush, Norman, Chen and Czugaj boarded a Jetstar flight from Bali to Darwin, wearing masks and civilian clothes, with Australian officials. ABC News said they were added to a list of people banned from ever returning to Indonesia. Albanese confirmed their arrival on social media and thanked Prabowo for his "compassion". The men said through a statement from their lawyer, Julian McMahon, that they were "relieved and happy" to be back, and were "immensely grateful" to the Indonesian president.

The legal description of what had happened was disputed. Indonesia's law minister, Yusril Ihza Mahendra, said the five were transferred as prisoners and were not granted clemency. Yet the ABC reported that legal experts in both countries had said a prisoner transfer was not possible because the laws did not exist, that a "practical agreement" was signed in a virtual meeting with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, and that the men were understood to be free. Indonesia's wish to monitor them in Australia could not be imposed, the broadcaster said. Albanese, for his part, said that the men had committed serious offences but that it was time for them to come home. The Australian ministers' statement said the men would have the chance to continue their rehabilitation and reintegration in Australia.
